title: Planning the Camino Francés: credential, stages and when to go
lead: Your first Camino, step by step: how to get a pilgrim passport, what the Compostela requires, Saint-Jean or Sarria, how public albergues work and when to cross the Pyrenees, from official sources.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The Camino Francés, or French Way, is the classic route of the Camino de Santiago. Galicia's official Xacobeo site calls it the Way of St James with the greatest historical tradition and the most internationally recognized, and it was already described in 1135 in the Codex Calixtinus, a medieval guide for pilgrims. From Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port in the French Pyrenees it runs about 780 km (roughly 485 miles) west across northern Spain, through Navarre, La Rioja, Castile and León and Galicia, to the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela.

You don't need a permit to walk it, and you don't need to walk it all at once. What you do need is a little planning: a pilgrim passport, a sensible starting point, a season that suits you and a plan for where to sleep. Here's how it works, using the rules as the Pilgrim's Office and Galicia's Xunta publish them.
Your pilgrim passport: the Credencial

The Credencial del Peregrino is the document you carry along the Way and get stamped as you go. The Pilgrim's Reception Office in Santiago lists where to get one: at the office itself (Rúa Carretas 33, Santiago de Compostela), at parish churches and dioceses, from Confraternities of St James and authorized pilgrim associations in Spain and around the world, at pilgrim hostels, and through an official digital version for Android and iOS. If you start in Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, the pilgrim welcome office there is at 39 rue de la Citadelle and helps walkers prepare before they set off.

According to the Pilgrim's Office, stamps are normally collected where you sleep, such as hostels, but you can also get them at parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. The office notes that the Credencial is meant for pilgrims on foot, by bicycle or on horseback who wish to make the pilgrimage with a Christian sentiment.
The Compostela and where to start
Photos from the trail

The Compostela is the certificate the Cathedral issues to pilgrims at the end of the Way. In the Pilgrim's Office's current wording, you need to complete at least 100 continuous kilometers on the same route to Santiago on foot or on horseback (at least 200 km by bicycle), and the last stage must be the one leading into Santiago's Cathedral. If you start outside Spain, at least 70 km of that distance must be in Spain. You show your duly stamped Credencial at the Pilgrim's Reception Office, and the Compostela is given to those who make the pilgrimage for Christian reasons.

That rule shapes the big choice: where to begin. Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port is the traditional start of the full Camino Francés, the last stop on the Way in France before the crossing into Spain. Spain's official tourism site, spain.info, points to Sarria as the popular starting point for a shorter walk because walking from there entitles you to the Compostela. Many people do neither end to end: spain.info notes that the Camino is usually done in sections and that most people spend about a week on it, which is usually enough for about 200 km (about 125 miles). Coming back in later years to continue is completely normal.
See the Camino Francés on the map, with route details, tips and photos from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port to Santiago.
Stages and how long it takes

Spain.info counts about 32 stages on the French Way, and its featured full itinerary from Saint-Jean to Santiago takes 38 days. Stage lengths and the number of days you need vary with your pace, rest days and where you choose to sleep, so treat any plan as a starting point and build in slack for sore feet.

The first stage is the hardest. Pays Basque tourism describes it as a 27 km (about 17 mile) mountain climb through the Basque Pyrenees to Roncesvalles, around 7 hours of walking, and spain.info calls it very difficult and physically demanding. Plan it as a full day. Further west, the Way enters Galicia at O Cebreiro; Xacobeo lists the Galician section at 155 km via San Xil or 162.2 km via Samos, passing Triacastela, Sarria, Portomarín, Palas de Rei, Melide and Arzúa on the way to Santiago.
Where to sleep: albergues

Pilgrim hostels, or albergues, are the backbone of the Camino, but spain.info notes you can also choose rural houses, hotels, Paradors, hostels and campsites. In Galicia, the Xunta runs a network of public albergues with clear published rules. Reservations are not accepted. Beds go in order of arrival, with priority given first to pilgrims with physical limitations, then walkers, then pilgrims on horseback, then cyclists, then people traveling with a support vehicle.

You can stay one night only, except in case of illness or force majeure, and the price is €10 per person per night. Doors open at 1:00 pm and close at 10:00 pm, lights go out at 10:30 pm (except in common areas), and you must leave before 8:00 am. Expect dormitories, hot showers, a kitchen and laundry facilities, with disposable bedding provided. In busy months, many pilgrims book private accommodation ahead for peace of mind.
When to go
You can walk the Camino at any time of year, but spain.info says it is especially pleasant in spring and from September to October, when temperatures are milder and there is less rain.

Winter also changes the first stage. The high Route Napoléon over the Pyrenees is closed from 1 November to 31 March, and Visit Navarra says that in those months the lower route through Luzaide/Valcarlos is the only possible route. Visit Navarra also recommends Valcarlos whenever the weather is bad, at any time of year. Mountain weather here can change fast, so check the forecast and current advice at the pilgrim office in Saint-Jean before you leave, and don't attempt the high route when it's closed.
Get your Credencial before you go, start slower than you think you need to, and let the weather choose your route over the Pyrenees.
Getting there and getting home

Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port is served by regional TER trains on the line from Bayonne in southwest France; check SNCF's TER Nouvelle-Aquitaine timetables, as replacement buses sometimes run. At the other end, spain.info notes that Santiago's airport is 10 km (about 6 miles) from the city, high-speed trains link Santiago with Madrid, and the bus station connects to other Galician cities and to countries including Portugal and France.
Safety and respect

Walking day after day for weeks is a real test of feet and stamina, so break in your footwear before you go, carry rain gear and warm layers for the mountains, and stick to the waymarked route. Respect the albergue rules and quiet hours, carry your rubbish out, and remember that churches and the Cathedral are places of worship as well as landmarks.
Another classic European long walk
If you're drawn to multi-week walking in Europe but want high mountains instead of a pilgrimage, the Tour du Mont Blanc circles the Mont Blanc massif through France, Italy and Switzerland.
Another classic European long walk: the Tour du Mont Blanc, a loop around the Alps' highest peak.

Rules, prices and route conditions change. Always check the current requirements with the Pilgrim's Reception Office (oficinadelperegrino.com) and Galicia's official Xacobeo site (caminodesantiago.gal) before you go.

title: Half Dome permits 2027: how the lottery works
lead: Preseason lottery, daily lottery, fees, group size and what to hike if you don't win: a step-by-step guide to Half Dome permits, using the rules NPS has published for the latest season.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Half Dome rises nearly 5,000 feet (about 1,520 m) above Yosemite Valley, and the last 400 feet (about 120 m) to its summit are climbed on two metal cables. To protect the wilderness, reduce crowding and improve safety, the National Park Service (NPS) requires a permit to hike to the top seven days a week whenever the cables are up. Day hiker permits are given out by lottery through Recreation.gov.

A quick note on dates: as of October 2026, NPS has not published anything specific to the 2027 season. Everything below is the process as NPS and Recreation.gov publish it for the 2026 season. The rules have a fixed yearly rhythm, but check nps.gov/yose for 2027 updates before you apply.
The season and the daily limit

NPS says the cables are normally up from the Friday before Memorial Day (the last Monday in May), and the last day to use them is the day after the second Monday in October. These dates can change with conditions, so check the park's current status. If the cables aren't up on the date of your permit, the per-person permit fee is refunded.

A maximum of 300 hikers a day are allowed on the Half Dome Trail beyond the base of the Sub Dome: about 225 day hikers and 75 backpackers. Rangers check permits at the base of the Sub Dome, so without a permit, that's where your hike ends.
Photos from the trail
Step 1: the preseason lottery (March)
Most permits go out in one preseason lottery. For the 2026 season it worked like this:

Application window: March 1 through March 31 (Eastern time), online at Recreation.gov or by phone at 877-444-6777. Permits: 225 for each day of the season. Group size: up to six permits (six people) per application. Dates: you can list specific dates or date ranges in priority order; Recreation.gov allows up to seven choices. Your application only wins if the full number of permits you asked for is available on at least one of your dates, and you're awarded the highest-priority date that works. Results: an email in mid-April, also available online or by calling Recreation.gov.

Fees: a $10 application fee, charged per application (not per person) and not refundable. If you win, there's a second fee of $10 per person. That one is fully refundable if you cancel by 11:59 pm Pacific time the day before your hike.

Name a permit holder and, if you can, an alternate, who must accept the role on Recreation.gov in time. Each person can appear on only one preseason application. Applying more than once gets all your applications canceled, and names can't be changed after you submit.
Step 2: the daily lottery (two days ahead)

If you miss out in March, there's a daily lottery all season long. How many permits there are depends on expected cancellations and no-shows, so it varies by day. You apply two days before your hike date, between midnight and 4 pm Pacific time. To hike on a Saturday, for example, you apply on Thursday. You'll get an email late that evening, and results are also online or by phone the next morning. Daily applications only allow a permit holder, with no alternate. The same $10 application fee and $10-per-person permit fee apply.
In 2024, NPS reports, 22% of preseason and 19% of daily applications won, with better daily odds on weekdays. Past odds don't predict future ones.
Flexible on dates? Pick weekdays, list every date you could make, and keep the daily lottery as your plan B.
What your permit covers

A day hiker permit lets your group go beyond the base of the Sub Dome and climb the Sub Dome steps and the cables, on the date shown on your permit only. It doesn't include any camping or lodging before, during or after your hike. Permits can't be transferred, and the permit holder or the alternate must be with the whole group at the base of the Sub Dome. Bring a photo ID and the email confirmation showing that the permit has been paid.

Backpacking? Don't use the day hiker lotteries if you're camping in Little Yosemite Valley or starting an overnight trip in Yosemite. Request Half Dome permits with your wilderness permit instead. NPS sets aside about 75 backpacker permits a day at $10 per person. Starting outside Yosemite? Then you need the day hiker lotteries.
Explore Yosemite National Park, including our Half Dome trail page, with maps and photos from the community.
No permit? Great Yosemite hikes that don't need one
Yosemite has plenty of big days that need no lottery. Here are the NPS figures:

Mist Trail to Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall: from near Happy Isles, it's 2.4 mi (3.9 km) round trip to the top of Vernal Fall, gaining 1,000 ft (300 m), about 3 hours. To the top of Nevada Fall via the Mist Trail it's 5.4 mi (8.7 km) round trip, gaining 2,000 ft (610 m), 5 to 6 hours. The Mist Trail's granite stairway has more than 600 steps, and spray makes it slippery in spring. NPS has limited the section along Vernal Fall to certain days in some seasons, so check before you go.

Upper Yosemite Fall: the Yosemite Falls Trail starts near Camp 4. It's 2 mi (3.2 km) round trip to Columbia Rock, gaining 1,000 ft, 2 to 3 hours. The full climb to the top of the fall is 7.2 mi (11.6 km) round trip, gaining 2,700 ft (823 m), 6 to 8 hours.

Clouds Rest: from the Sunrise Lakes trailhead on Tioga Road, it's 14 mi (22.5 km) round trip, gaining 2,300 ft (700 m), 8 to 10 hours, to a 9,926 ft (3,025 m) summit with 360-degree views. You can only drive to the trailhead when Tioga Road is open. NPS says that's typically late May or early June until sometime in October or November.
Safety on the cables

The full Half Dome hike is 14 to 16 miles (22.5 to 26 km) round trip, with about 4,800 feet (1,460 m) of elevation gain. Most people take 10 to 12 hours. NPS suggests leaving around sunrise and setting a firm turnaround time. Carry a headlamp with extra batteries (a phone doesn't count). Bring at least 1 gallon (4 liters) of water per person. Sturdy, grippy gloves help on the cables, but pack them out.

Don't go up the cables if the rock is wet. NPS says nearly all fatal falls from the cables happened in wet conditions, when the rock and cables are very slick. Don't climb when storm clouds are around either. The summit is dangerous in lightning, and thunderstorms are most common in the afternoon but can happen at any time. If a storm comes close, don't keep going. If you're on top, leave the summit area, carefully.

Permit rules, fees and dates can change from year to year. Before you apply, and again before you hike, check the current Half Dome rules and conditions with Yosemite National Park at nps.gov/yose and the lottery details at Recreation.gov.

title: How to plan the Tour du Mont Blanc
lead: One loop, three countries and around 170 km of Alpine trail: how direction, stages, refuge bookings, season, transport and mountain safety work on the Tour du Mont Blanc, based on the official TMB sources and local tourism offices.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB) is a long-distance loop around the Mont Blanc massif, passing through France, Italy and Switzerland. The official TMB website describes it as about 170 km (roughly 105 miles) with around 10,000 m (about 32,800 feet) of elevation gain. Other official sources give slightly different totals depending on the exact line they measure, so treat these as round numbers rather than a precise count.

You don't need technical climbing skills, but you do need stamina. The official FAQ says you should be able to walk 5 to 8 hours a day for several days in a row while carrying a pack. Here's how to put a trip together.
Direction and where to start

You can walk the loop either way. The official FAQ notes that the anticlockwise direction is the most common and the best waymarked, so it's the natural choice for a first TMB. Les Houches, just down the valley from Chamonix, is the classic start, but the official route page lists several other starting points, including Chamonix, Les Contamines, Courmayeur, Champex, La Fouly and Trient.

Going anticlockwise from Les Houches, the route heads over the Col de Voza to Les Contamines-Montjoie, crosses the Col du Bonhomme area to Les Chapieux, then climbs the Col de la Seigne into Italy. It drops through Val Veny to Courmayeur, follows the balconies above Val Ferret and crosses the Grand Col Ferret (2,537 m) into Switzerland. The Swiss section links La Fouly, Champex-Lac and Trient before the trail returns to France over the Col de Balme and traverses back above the Chamonix valley to Les Houches.
See the Tour du Mont Blanc on our map, with photos of the trail from our community.
Photos from the trail
Stages and days

According to the official TMB site, the tour is usually walked in 10 to 11 stages, each a day's walk between two places to sleep. Stages typically run 10 to 20 km, and some ascents exceed 1,000 m. The site suggests three rough paces: about 7 days for experienced, fast hikers; 9 to 10 days for a balanced trip, the most popular option; and 11 to 12 days for a slower, more contemplative tour. Pick your pace first, because it decides where you need beds each night.
Booking refuges

Book your nights before you set off. The official TMB site warns that in high season refuges and guesthouses are often full several months in advance. Its booking platform lets you build your route stage by stage across all three countries, choosing between dormitories, private rooms and camping.

For summer 2027, the official FAQ says bookings open on 15 October 2026 for all of the association's member refuges. You pay a deposit when you book. If you cancel more than 30 days before arrival, 80% of the deposit is refunded; less than 30 days out, it isn't refunded unless your insurance covers it. You can change a booking through your account up to 30 days before arrival. The FAQ gives a guide price of around €65 to €95 per night for half-board in a dormitory. Check current terms and prices when you book.
Choose your pace, lock in your refuges the day bookings open, then plan your trains and buses around them.
When to go

The official recommendation is mid-June to mid-September, when the passes are usually free of snow and the refuges are open. July and August bring the most stable conditions. In June and early July you may still meet snow patches, and the official guidance notes that in June and September signposting may be incomplete and some stream crossings harder. Later in the season, pack for colder weather.
Getting to Chamonix and Les Houches

The Chamonix tourism office lists Geneva International Airport as the nearest major airport, 88 km away, with daily bus connections to Chamonix. By rail, the Mont Blanc Express line runs from Saint-Gervais-les-Bains-Le Fayet to Martigny in Switzerland, stopping at Les Houches, Chamonix, Argentière and Vallorcine. The Chamonix Mobilité bus network also serves the valley, including Les Houches.

Public transport also lets you join or leave the loop partway. The official TMB site mentions free shuttles in Val Veny and Val Ferret on the Italian side, and the Pays du Saint-Bernard tourism office suggests the train to Orsières and then a bus to Champex-Lac on the Swiss side. Note that dogs aren't allowed on the shuttles.
Variants worth knowing

The official route lists several variants, from the Col de Tricot on the first stage to the Col des Fours near Les Chapieux and the high balcony via the Malatra pass above Val Ferret. The best known is the Fenêtre d'Arpette (2,665 m) between Champex-Lac and the Col de la Forclaz. The official TMB site calls it one of the finest and most demanding variants, for seasoned hikers comfortable on rocky ground and long descents. In bad weather, mist or when you're tired, take the classic route instead.
Three countries, three sets of rules

Crossing borders on foot is part of the TMB's charm, but the rules change with the country. Camping and bivouacking are a good example. The official TMB site explains that in France the rules vary by municipality, and Chamonix bans camping and bivouacking except for high-altitude overnight stays. All forms of camping are banned across Italy's Aosta Valley, and bivouacking there is forbidden below 2,500 m. In Switzerland's Valais, bivouacking is generally banned with a few tightly controlled exceptions, and camping is only allowed at designated sites. If you plan to carry a tent, read the official rules for each section first.
Mountain safety and weather

Alpine weather changes fast. The official TMB site advises checking the forecast the evening before and again in the morning, keeping a warm layer and waterproof jacket within reach, and setting off early so you don't reach high passes like the Col de la Seigne in mid-afternoon when storms are forecast. On early-season snowfields it recommends crampons, an ice axe and poles, and warns that snow bridges over streams can collapse. Good boots, a map, a whistle and a first aid kit belong in every pack.

There is no mobile network between Pont Romain and the Col de la Seigne via the Chapieux valley. In an emergency, 112 works in all three countries; Switzerland also uses 144. The PGHM mountain rescue service in Chamonix is on +33 4 50 53 16 89.

Trails change from year to year. In 2026, for example, the official site announced a diversion on the Swiss section because of rockfall danger. Before and during your trip, check trail conditions on autourdumontblanc.com, ask La Chamoniarde's mountain office in Chamonix, and follow Météo-France's mountain forecasts.
More Alpine classics
If the TMB gets you hooked on the Alps, the Italian Dolomites are a natural next trip.

title: Climbing Kilimanjaro: routes, rules and acclimatisation
lead: Huts or tents, five days or eight, south, west or north: how the routes up Africa's highest mountain differ, why more days on the mountain help, and the park rules every climber needs to know, from Tanzania National Parks and the CDC.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa's highest peak and, as Tanzania National Parks (TANAPA) puts it, the world's tallest free-standing mountain. Its summit, Uhuru Peak on the Kibo cone, stands at 5,895 m (19,341 feet). The massif is made of three volcanoes: Kibo and Mawenzi (5,149 m), which are dormant, and Shira (3,962 m), an extinct volcano whose collapse formed the wide Shira Plateau. Kilimanjaro National Park was declared in 1973 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

You don't need technical climbing skills to reach the top on the standard routes, but you do need to pick a route, a licensed operator and, above all, enough days. Here's how the options compare, using what the park authority and the CDC publish.
The ground rules: licensed operators only

TANAPA is clear that all climbs must be guided by a licensed operator, and solo trekking is not permitted. Guide and porter services are arranged through licensed tour operators, who also handle transfers from Moshi or Arusha to the park gates. Most climbers fly into Kilimanjaro International Airport (JRO) or Arusha Airport (ARK).

On the mountain, the park asks you to stay on marked routes, follow camp rules and ranger or guide instructions, and practice Leave No Trace. Off-trail travel and open fires are restricted, and drones need prior authorization. TANAPA also encourages climbers to support local livelihoods by choosing licensed operators with fair porter practices, which is worth asking about when you compare companies.

Fees depend on your visitor category (citizen, resident or non-resident), your route and the number of days, and conservation, camping or hut, and rescue fees may apply. Your operator usually bundles these into the trip price, but TANAPA recommends confirming the current Kilimanjaro fee schedule before you travel.
Photos from the trail
How the routes differ

TANAPA says six trails lead to the summit and that reaching Kibo peak takes 5 to 8 days, depending on the route. The park's own advice is short and worth remembering: the more days, the higher your chance of reaching the summit. The main gates are Marangu, Machame, Lemosho (reached via Londorossi) and Rongai on the north side, and Mweka Gate is used for the descent.

Marangu is the hut route. It is the only route TANAPA describes with alpine huts, at Mandara, Horombo and Kibo, so you sleep under a roof instead of in a tent. The park's headquarters is also at Marangu. If camping at altitude doesn't appeal to you, this is the route to look at, but check how many days your operator plans, since a short itinerary leaves little time to acclimatise.

Machame and Lemosho are camping routes. On every route except Marangu, climbers stay in designated tented camps run by licensed operators. Machame starts from its own gate, while Lemosho is reached via Londorossi. Ask each operator how many nights their itinerary spends on the mountain and how quickly it gains height, since that matters more than the name of the route.

Rongai is the northern option, starting from the Rongai gate on the north side of the mountain. Beyond the main trekking routes, TANAPA also lists a Crater Camp near the summit (special permit required), guided day hikes on the Marangu and Shira areas for non-summit visitors, and technical climbing on Mawenzi for highly skilled climbers.
Explore Kilimanjaro National Park on the map and see photos of the Roof of Africa from our community.
Acclimatisation: the real success factor

Kilimanjaro's challenge is altitude, not technique. The CDC notes that any unacclimatised traveler going to a sleeping altitude of 2,450 m (8,000 feet) or higher, and sometimes lower, is at risk of altitude illness. The summit sits more than twice that high.

The CDC's core advice is to ascend gradually. Once above 3,000 m (9,800 feet), it recommends increasing your sleeping altitude by no more than 500 m (1,650 feet) per night, and adding an extra night to acclimatise for every 1,000 m (3,300 feet) of sleeping altitude gained. It also advises avoiding alcohol for the first 48 hours at high altitude. TANAPA's safety guidance says the same thing in plain terms: choose an itinerary with acclimatisation days, ascend slowly, stay hydrated and report symptoms to your guide promptly.

Know the warning signs. According to the CDC, headache is the main symptom of acute mountain sickness, usually with loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue or nausea. Confusion, poor coordination and drowsiness can signal high-altitude cerebral edema, while a cough, chest congestion and unusual breathlessness on exertion can be early signs of high-altitude pulmonary edema. The CDC says you should never go up to sleep higher while you have symptoms, and if symptoms get worse despite treatment at the same altitude, descent is mandatory.

Medicines can help prevent altitude illness, but they are a conversation for your doctor, not a packing-list item. The CDC advises travelers with underlying medical conditions to see a physician familiar with high-altitude issues before the trip.
Pick the route for the days, not the days for the route. Extra nights on the mountain are the best summit insurance you can buy.
Seasons, weather and what to pack

TANAPA lists the park as open year-round. The climb passes through very different zones, from montane forest with colobus and blue monkeys, through heath and moorland with giant lobelias and groundsels, to alpine desert and the summit icefields. The park warns that conditions change quickly at high altitude, so talk to your licensed operator about the best months for your chosen route and check the forecast close to your dates.

Whatever the month, TANAPA asks climbers to carry proper cold-weather and rain gear, a headlamp and personal medications. Think warm layers and an insulated jacket for summit night, a waterproof shell for the forest, broken-in boots, good socks and a comfortable daypack for the things you'll carry while porters handle the rest.
Pair the climb with a safari
Many climbers fly into northern Tanzania once and stay for the wildlife afterwards. Serengeti National Park is also run by TANAPA, so you'll deal with the same park authority for rules and fees.
See Serengeti National Park, the classic way to rest your legs after the summit.

Routes, fees, regulations and conditions change. Always check the current rules and fee schedule with Tanzania National Parks at tanzaniaparks.go.tz/kilimanjaro, and review the CDC's altitude illness guidance with your doctor before you go.

title: Hiking into the Grand Canyon: rim to river, safely
lead: South Kaibab or Bright Angel, where day hikers should turn around, why the National Park Service warns against rim-to-river-and-back in one day, and how heat, water, permits and Phantom Ranch fit into your plan.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Walking below the rim of the Grand Canyon is nothing like hiking a mountain. You go down first, while you're fresh and the air is cool, and the hard part comes last, uphill and often in the heat. The National Park Service (NPS) puts it bluntly: there are no easy trails into or out of the Grand Canyon, and more than 300 people are rescued from the canyon each year.
Here's how the two main South Rim trails compare and where day hikers should turn around, with details from the park's own pages.
First: check what's open right now

After a significant flash flood on August 29, 2026, the park closed the whole of Phantom Ranch, including Bright Angel Campground, the canteen and the cabins. Also closed are the South Kaibab Trail below the Tipoff, the River Trail east of the River Resthouse, the Black and Silver bridges, and the entire North Kaibab Trail. As of the park's September 28, 2026 update, there is no estimated reopening date. The Bright Angel Trail is open from the trailhead down to the River Resthouse, along with Plateau Point and the Tonto Trail between the Tipoff and Havasupai Gardens. Check the park's Key Hiking Messages page before you plan anything.
Photos from the trail
South Kaibab vs Bright Angel

The South Kaibab Trail starts south of Yaki Point and follows a ridgeline down, which gives it some of the best views for a relatively short hike. That exposure comes at a cost: NPS describes it as steep, with little shade and no water along the trail. You can't drive to the trailhead: take the Kaibab Rim (Orange) Route shuttle from the Visitor Center, or arrive on foot or by bike. NPS lists 7 miles (11.3 km) from the trailhead to Bright Angel Campground.

The Bright Angel Trail starts in Grand Canyon Village, just west of Bright Angel Lodge. It's also steep, but it has some shade and, in normal years, seasonal water. It's the longer way down: NPS lists 4.5 miles (7.3 km) to Havasupai Gardens, 8 miles (12.9 km) to the River Resthouse and 9.5 miles (15.3 km) to Bright Angel Campground.
Explore Grand Canyon National Park on the map and see photos of the South Rim from our community.
Day-hike turnaround points

On the South Kaibab Trail, NPS suggests Ooh Aah Point (1.8 miles / 2.9 km round trip, 1 to 2 hours, 790 feet of elevation change), Cedar Ridge (3 miles / 4.8 km round trip, 2 to 4 hours, 1,120 feet) or Skeleton Point (6 miles / 9.6 km round trip, 4 to 6 hours, 2,040 feet). Cedar Ridge has pit toilets but no water. NPS does not recommend hiking below Skeleton Point as a day hike, because of the long distance, extreme temperature changes and an elevation change of about 5,000 feet each way.

On the Bright Angel Trail, the classic turnarounds are the Mile-and-a-Half Resthouse (3 miles / 4.8 km round trip, 2 to 4 hours, 1,120 feet) and the Three-Mile Resthouse (6 miles / 9.6 km round trip, 4 to 6 hours, 2,120 feet). Havasupai Gardens (9 miles / 14.4 km round trip, 6 to 9 hours, 3,040 feet) and Plateau Point (12 miles / 19.6 km round trip, 9 to 12 hours, 3,080 feet) are long, serious days. NPS says destinations below Havasupai Gardens are not recommended day hikes.
A simple rule from the park: allow one third of your time to go down and two thirds to come back up.
Do not attempt to hike from the rim to the river and back in one day, especially between May and September, when extreme heat can quickly become life-threatening.
Heat: the biggest danger

The inner canyon is far hotter than the rim. NPS says July shade temperatures at Phantom Ranch reach 104°F, and that sun temperatures run 15 to 20°F hotter than posted shade temperatures. Rangers strongly discourage hiking during the heat of the day, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., when most emergency heat cases happen. Start early, rest in the shade at midday and soak yourself whenever you're near water.

Know the warning signs. Heat exhaustion brings fatigue, nausea, vomiting, cool moist skin, headache and cramps: stop hiking, rest in the shade, drink water with electrolytes and eat. Heat stroke, with a flushed face, dry skin, a weak rapid pulse and confusion, is an emergency: cool the person immediately and call for help. Drinking lots of water without enough salt can cause hyponatremia, which looks like heat exhaustion. The treatment is to stop drinking water, eat salty food and rest in the shade.
Water and food

There is no water on the South Kaibab Trail. On the Bright Angel Trail, NPS says water is normally available from May through October at the Mile-and-a-Half and Three-Mile Resthouses, and year-round at Havasupai Gardens, but the pipeline is subject to breaks. Right now the park lists water as off at all three of those stops. Potable water is available in tanks at both trailheads. Carry all the water you need, plus purification tablets, and check water status at the Visitor Center or Backcountry Information Center on the day.
Food matters too. NPS says to eat about twice as much as you normally would, favoring salty snacks to balance your water intake.
Going overnight: permits and Phantom Ranch

If you want to reach the river, NPS's answer is to make it an overnight trip. Day hikes, including night-time ones, need no permit, but camping anywhere outside the developed rim campgrounds requires a backcountry permit. Apply through Recreation.gov: an early-access lottery opens on the 16th of the month, four months before your desired start month, and closes at 5 p.m. MST on the 1st. NPS lists a $10 permit or application fee plus $15 per person per night below the rim.

Phantom Ranch, at the bottom of the canyon, offers dormitories and cabins, with meals available for purchase. You don't need a backcountry permit to stay there, but you do need advance reservations, made through an online lottery run by Xanterra Parks and Resorts 15 months ahead. Phantom Ranch is closed after the August 2026 flood, so check its status before entering any lottery.
Seasons

Summer brings extreme heat below the rim, and NPS's strongest warnings cover May to September. Summer storms also bring lightning danger. In winter and early spring, the upper trails can be extremely icy. NPS says packed snow and ice is regularly found on the first three miles of the Bright Angel Trail, and the north-facing Chimney at the top of the South Kaibab holds ice all winter. The park recommends over-the-shoe traction devices, hiking poles and a flashlight with spare batteries.
More canyon country
Looking for more big-park hiking? Try Zion or Yosemite.
See Zion National Park, with towering sandstone cliffs and narrow canyons in southern Utah.
See Yosemite National Park, with granite walls, waterfalls and giant sequoias in California's Sierra Nevada.

Trail closures, water status and heat risk change often. Always check current conditions and regulations with Grand Canyon National Park at nps.gov/grca, and talk to a ranger before any long hike below the rim.

title: Hiking in the Dolomites: the Tre Cime loop and hut-to-hut basics
lead: The classic loop around the Tre Cime di Lavaredo, how the reservation-only toll road works in 2026, what to expect in an Italian rifugio, and a first look at the Alta Via 1, using details published by the local authorities and the Italian Alpine Club (CAI).
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The Dolomites were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List on 26 June 2009, for the beauty of their landscape and their geological importance. The site is a series of nine separate mountain systems, and the Tre Cime di Lavaredo (Drei Zinnen in German) sit in the Northern Dolomites system, on the border between the Veneto region and South Tyrol. Their three towers are probably the most photographed peaks in the range, and walking around them is a great first taste of Dolomites hiking.
This guide covers the loop itself, how to get to the trailhead under the 2026 rules, how mountain huts (rifugi) work, and the bigger multi-day route many hikers move on to: the Alta Via 1.
The Tre Cime loop

The loop starts at Rifugio Auronzo, on the south side of the peaks. The 3 Zinnen Dolomites tourism board lists the round trip as 8.8 km (about 5.5 miles), around 4 hours of walking, with about 550 m (about 1,800 feet) of ascent and descent. It rates the hike as easy, on well-kept trails.

From Rifugio Auronzo, trail no. 101 passes Rifugio Lavaredo and climbs gradually to Forcella Lavaredo (Paternsattel), about an hour from the start. This is where the 500-metre-high north faces of the three peaks come into view. Beyond the saddle the trail dips under Monte Paterno to a fork: one branch climbs easily to Rifugio Locatelli (Dreizinnenhütte), while trail no. 105 heads to the Langalm hut and its lake, then back along the west side of the peaks to the start.
See the Tre Cime di Lavaredo on the map, with photos of the north faces from our community.
Photos from the trail
Getting there: the toll road in 2026

The road up from Misurina to the Rifugio Auronzo car park is managed by the Municipality of Auronzo di Cadore. Since summer 2025, cars can only reach the car park with an online reservation made through the official portal, auronzo.info. The portal shows available days and time slots in real time. When booking, you give an email address, a phone number and the license plate of the vehicle.

The municipality reopened the road for the 2026 season on 23 May 2026. Its published 2026 rates are €40 per car, €26 per motorcycle and €60 per camper or motorhome. The local tourism consortium says the road is generally open from late May to late October, weather permitting.

Prefer not to drive? The tourism board points to the line 444 shuttle bus from Dobbiaco/Toblach via Misurina to Rifugio Auronzo, and the Auronzo-Misurina consortium runs local buses from June. Timetables and booking rules change each season, so check the South Tyrol public transport site (sii.bz.it) and the consortium's website before you go. You can also hike in on foot from the valleys, for example from Landro in the Rienza valley or from the Fischleintal and Innerfeldtal valleys near Sexten and Innichen.
How rifugi work

Rifugi are staffed mountain huts that serve meals and, at many of them, offer beds in shared rooms. Rifugio Auronzo, for example, is run directly by the local CAI section of Auronzo. Huts owned by the Italian Alpine Club follow a common set of rules, and they are a good guide to etiquette across the range.

Under the CAI rules, booking a bed is recommended for everyone and required for groups of more than ten. You can book through the hut's own channels (website, phone or email) or the CAI's Prenota Rifugi platform, and a booking only counts once the hut manager confirms it. Unless you agree otherwise, your bed is held until 6 pm on your arrival day, so call ahead if you're running late. The manager may ask for a deposit of up to one night's price.

Once you're there, a few house rules apply. Leave your climbing gear in the dedicated room or outside, and take your boots off indoors. A personal sleeping sheet (sacco lenzuolo) is mandatory for overnight stays; ask the manager if you don't have one. Respect quiet hours, keep noise down on early starts, fold your blankets, and carry out all your trash. Smoking, music speakers and drying clothes on heaters are not allowed. CAI members get discounted rates, so if you plan several hut nights in Italy, it may be worth joining CAI or a club with a reciprocal agreement.
Book the road and the beds before anything else, bring a sleeping sheet, and plan to be off high ground before the afternoon storms build.
Going further: the Alta Via 1

If the Tre Cime loop leaves you wanting more, the Alta Via 1 is the classic hut-to-hut route through the eastern Dolomites. The CAI describes it as about 125 km (about 78 miles) with around 7,300 m of elevation gain, running from Lago di Braies (Pragser Wildsee) to the city of Belluno in 12 stages. Along the way it links rifugi such as Biella, Fanes, Lagazuoi, Nuvolau, Croda da Lago, Vazzoler, Carestiato, Sommariva, Pian de Fontana and 7° Alpini.

The CAI calls the main route not particularly challenging for a good hiker, with fixed aids on the hardest sections. Optional variants add via ferrata sections and summits for more experienced hikers. Plan to book each night in advance and check each hut's opening dates.
Like the idea of walking hut to hut? The Tour du Mont Blanc is another classic Alpine circuit.
A note on via ferrata

Many Dolomites routes include via ferrata, protected climbing paths with fixed steel cables and ladders. They are not hiking trails. CAI safety material says you need certified gear and must know how to use it: a climbing helmet, a harness and a via ferrata energy-absorbing set built to the EN 958 standard. Put your helmet on first, because rockfall from climbers above is common. Modern textile absorbers can't be reused after a fall. Avoid via ferrata in rain, snow, wind or when storms threaten. If you're new to it, go with a certified mountain guide.
Weather and thunderstorms

The CAI warns that summer thunderstorms, especially heat-driven ones, are a serious risk in the mountains. In unstable conditions, cumulus clouds can grow quickly through the morning and break into storms in the afternoon. Check a reliable, up-to-date forecast before you set out, start early, and watch the sky. If a storm hits, look for shelter right away and stay clear of isolated trees, exposed rock, ridges and metal objects. The 3 Zinnen tourism board names June to September as the main hiking season, with quieter trails and strong colors in autumn.
More Italian classics
Want to pair the mountains with the sea? The coastal paths between the five villages of the Cinque Terre make a great contrast to a week in the Dolomites.
Explore Cinque Terre National Park, with cliffside trails between colorful villages on the Ligurian coast.

title: The best lake hikes in Banff
lead: Turquoise water, tea houses and larch forests: the best lake hikes around Lake Louise, Moraine Lake and Banff, with Parks Canada's distances, the 2026 shuttle and parking rules, and bear safety.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Banff National Park is famous for its lakes: milky turquoise water under glaciers, ringed by trails that range from flat shoreline walks to steep climbs into larch forest. All distances, elevations and times come from Parks Canada's Banff trail descriptions, and all transport and parking details come from Parks Canada's 2026 visitor information.
Parks Canada lists distances one way unless a trail is a loop, and times as round trips; we've added rough miles and feet.
Lake Louise: Lake Agnes and the Plain of Six Glaciers

Both of Lake Louise's classic hikes start at the Lake Louise Lakeshore parking lot, 4 km from the community of Lake Louise. If you only want a gentle walk, the Lake Louise Lakeshore Trail runs 2.3 km (about 1.4 miles) one way to the far end of the lake, where you'll see the milky creek that gives the water its colour. Parks Canada estimates about an hour round trip.

Lake Agnes Trail: 3.9 km (about 2.4 miles) one way, 495 m (about 1,620 feet) of elevation gain, 2.5 to 3 hours round trip. A well-maintained trail climbs to a lake tucked under towering peaks, with a seasonal European-style tea house. From Lake Agnes you can add the Big Beehive (1.5 km one way, 150 m gain) for a panorama of Lake Louise and the Chateau, or the Little Beehive (0.9 km one way, 65 m gain), a former fire lookout site with views of the Bow Valley.

Plain of Six Glaciers Trail: 5.9 km (about 3.7 miles) one way, 595 m (about 1,950 feet) of gain, about 4 hours round trip. It runs beyond the end of Lake Louise toward big peaks and glaciers, and also has a seasonal Swiss-built tea house. Feeling strong? Parks Canada notes you can link Lake Agnes and the Plain of Six Glaciers via the Highline Trail into a 14.3 km (about 8.9 mile) loop of around 5 hours.
See Banff National Park on the map, with photos of its lakes and peaks from our community.
Photos from the trail
Moraine Lake: Rockpile, Consolation Lakes and Larch Valley

Moraine Lake sits in the Valley of the Ten Peaks. For the famous view, the Rockpile Loop is a 0.7 km (about 0.4 mile) loop with 35 m of gain, about 30 minutes. Parks Canada asks visitors to stay safe and not climb on the rocks. The Moraine Lake Lakeshore Trail is an easy 1.3 km (about 0.8 mile) stroll with views of Mount Fay and the Fay Glacier, about 45 minutes round trip.
Consolation Lakes Trail: 2.9 km (about 1.8 miles) one way, 135 m of gain, about 2 hours round trip, with views of alpine meadows, scree slopes and the Quadra Glacier.

Larch Valley/Minnestimma Lakes Trail: 4.5 km (about 2.8 miles) one way, 570 m (about 1,870 feet) of gain, 3.5 to 4 hours round trip, climbing into a larch forest high above the lake with views of the Ten Peaks. From there, Sentinel Pass via Larch Valley is a difficult 5.6 km (about 3.5 miles) one way with 750 m (about 2,460 feet) of gain and steep switchbacks, 4.5 to 5.5 hours round trip.
Book the shuttle first, pick the hike second, and carry bear spray on your hip, not in your pack.
Getting to the lakes: shuttles and parking in 2026

Moraine Lake Road is closed to personal vehicles year-round. You can reach Moraine Lake only by Parks Canada shuttle, Roam public transit connections or a licensed commercial operator; registered guests of Moraine Lake Lodge are the exception. In 2026, Parks Canada shuttles ran to Lake Louise Lakeshore from May 15 and to Moraine Lake from June 1 (weather permitting), both until October 12, with a Lake Connector shuttle between the two lakes.

Shuttle reservations opened at 8 am MT on April 15, 2026, with 40% of seats released then. The other 60% are released on a rolling basis at 8 am MT two days (48 hours) before each departure. Book online or at 1-877-737-3783. Regular shuttles leave the Lake Louise Park and Ride at the Lake Louise Ski Resort (1 Whitehorn Road) (free parking with a reservation) every 30 minutes from 6:30 am to 5 pm; the last return is at 7:30 pm. Parks Canada lists 2026 fares of CA$12.75 per adult, CA$6.00 for seniors and CA$4.00 for youth, plus a non-refundable reservation fee (CA$3.50 online, CA$5.50 by phone). Early starters can book the Alpine Start shuttle, which leaves from the upper Lake Louise Lakeshore lot at 4 am and 5 am; reserve by 3 pm the day before and pay for parking there.

Driving to Lake Louise? Paid parking is in effect at Lake Louise Lakeshore during the shuttle season, 3 am to 7 pm, at a 2026 day rate of CA$42 per vehicle, payable on site only. Parks Canada warns the lot often fills before sunrise, and you may be turned around when traffic is too heavy. Vehicles longer than 6 m (20 feet) or wider than 2 m (79 inches) can't park there.
Near the town of Banff: Johnson Lake

Johnson Lake Loop: a 2.9 km (about 1.8 mile) loop with 90 m of gain, about an hour. It is a rolling circuit with views of Cascade Mountain and Mount Rundle, passing some of Alberta's oldest Douglas fir trees. The trailhead is at the Johnson Lake Day-use Area, 12 km east of Banff off Lake Minnewanka Road, and Roam Route 6 serves it in summer.
Bear safety

Banff is grizzly and black bear country. Parks Canada's advice on trails is to travel in tight groups of four or more, stay alert, make noise, carry bear spray and know how to use it. Keep the spray in a holster you can reach with your dominant hand, not in your pack, and check the expiry date. Parks Canada calls it a last resort for a bear acting aggressively at close range. Bear spray is not allowed on commercial airlines, even in checked baggage, so buy it after you arrive.

Moraine Lake area trails are among those where Parks Canada routinely uses seasonal access restrictions. Group Access requires a tight group of at least four hikers, close enough that the person in front can comfortably talk to the person at the back. Ignoring a restriction can bring charges under the National Parks Regulations, with a maximum fine of CA$25,000.
When to go

Mountain weather changes quickly, and Parks Canada notes it can snow in any month. Parks Canada warns that the moderate and difficult Lake Louise and Moraine Lake area trails, including Lake Agnes, the Plain of Six Glaciers and Larch Valley, are exposed to avalanche hazard, and travel is not recommended from mid-October to mid-June. Pack layers, a rain jacket and hiking poles, plus ice cleats for icy trails. Cell coverage is not reliable, so consider a satellite messenger.
Love granite, waterfalls and big-wall views too? Explore Yosemite National Park from our community.
Just south of the border, Glacier National Park has the same lake-and-peak drama on the Highline Trail.

Trail conditions, closures, bear restrictions, shuttle dates and fees change often. Always check current trail conditions, important bulletins and regulations with Parks Canada at parks.canada.ca/banff before you go.

title: Glacier National Park's best day hikes, from the Highline Trail to Grinnell Glacier
lead: Six classic day hikes in Montana's Glacier National Park, with official trail figures, the 2026 Logan Pass shuttle and parking rules, and the bear safety basics every hiker needs, straight from the National Park Service.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: Glacier National Park in northwest Montana is a place of jagged peaks, turquoise lakes, wildflower meadows and, yes, glaciers. Much of its best scenery sits right off Going-to-the-Sun Road or in valleys like Many Glacier and Two Medicine, which makes it one of the great day-hiking parks in North America.

Here are six classic day hikes, with distances and elevation figures as the National Park Service (NPS) publishes them, plus how access works in 2026. One big change first: the park has moved away from vehicle reservations and toward a ticketed shuttle and timed parking at Logan Pass.
Getting in: 2026 access rules

Vehicle reservations are not required in 2026. The NPS says they will not be required at Many Glacier, Two Medicine, the North Fork or on Going-to-the-Sun Road. The park notes that temporary diversions may happen when areas reach capacity, and that visitors with lodging, camping or tour reservations get entry priority.

Logan Pass is where things are different. From July 1 through Labor Day (September 7, 2026), private vehicle parking at Logan Pass is limited to three hours, enforced 24 hours a day. After parking, you take a free, timestamped permit from the kiosk and put it on your dashboard. Overnight parking is not allowed, except for permitted backcountry users and Granite Park Chalet guests. The NPS says three hours should be enough for the Hidden Lake Overlook, but Highline Trail hikers will need a shuttle ticket.

The Logan Pass Shuttle runs over the same dates. A $1 ticket is required for each person over 2 years old, and tickets are sold only on Recreation.gov or by phone at 877-444-6777, not in the park. Tickets open 60 days in advance at 8 a.m. MDT (starting May 2), with more released at 7 p.m. MDT the night before (starting June 30). West-side shuttles board at the Apgar Visitor Center and Lake McDonald Lodge; east-side shuttles board at the St. Mary Visitor Center and Rising Sun Picnic Area. Note that Avalanche Lake and Trail of the Cedars are not accessible by park shuttle in 2026.
Explore Glacier National Park on the map and see photos from our community.
Photos from the trail
1. Highline Trail

The Highline is Glacier's signature hike. It starts across Going-to-the-Sun Road from the Continental Divide sign near the Logan Pass parking lot and usually ends at The Loop. The NPS lists it at 11.8 miles (19 km) one way, with 2,388 ft (728 m) of gain and 4,773 ft (1,455 m) of loss. Optional side trips lead to Grinnell Glacier Overlook, Swiftcurrent Lookout and Granite Park Chalet, which change the totals.

The NPS warns that much of the trail is exposed, which means a higher risk of falling and of being caught by bad weather. Because it's a point-to-point hike, plan your return: the shuttle stops at The Loop in both directions, with afternoon pickups roughly every 60 to 90 minutes. The park says there is no other public transportation back from Logan Pass if you miss the last shuttle.
2. Hidden Lake Overlook

Also starting at Logan Pass, this is the best short hike on the road. The NPS lists the overlook at 1.3 miles (2.1 km) one way with 608 ft (185 m) of gain, on a mix of wooden boardwalk and packed soil. Continuing down to Hidden Lake itself makes it 2.5 miles (4 km) one way with 639 ft (195 m) of gain. It fits inside the three-hour parking window.
3. Avalanche Lake

On the west side of Going-to-the-Sun Road, Avalanche Lake starts off the Trail of the Cedars near the Avalanche Picnic Area. The NPS lists it at 2.3 miles (3.7 km) one way, with 741 ft (226 m) of gain and 275 ft (84 m) of loss, climbing through old-growth forest to an alpine lake with waterfalls pouring in. It's very popular, and since the shuttle doesn't serve it in 2026, plan to drive and arrive early.
4. Grinnell Glacier

In the Many Glacier valley, this is the hike that takes you closest to one of the park's namesake glaciers. From the Grinnell Glacier Trailhead, the NPS lists the viewpoint at 5.0 miles (8.0 km) one way, with 2,596 ft (791 m) of gain and 1,015 ft (309 m) of loss. You can shorten it by booking concessioner boat tickets from Many Glacier Hotel, which drop you 1.3 miles (2.1 km) closer: 3.7 miles (6.0 km) one way, with 2,461 ft (750 m) of gain. Expect wildflowers, big views and a mostly exposed trail.
5. Iceberg Lake

Also in Many Glacier, Iceberg Lake starts at the Iceberg-Ptarmigan Trailhead behind the Swiftcurrent Motor Inn. The NPS lists it at 4.8 miles (7.7 km) one way, with 1,765 ft (538 m) of gain and 624 ft (190 m) of loss, ending at a turquoise lake known for its ice floes.
6. Scenic Point

For a quieter corner of the park, head to Two Medicine. The Scenic Point Trailhead is 0.3 miles (0.5 km) east of the Two Medicine Ranger Station, and the NPS lists the hike at 3.8 miles (6.1 km) one way with 2,259 ft (689 m) of gain. It's a steady, mostly exposed climb, so bring sun protection and a wind layer.
Carry bear spray, make noise, and know how you're getting back before you set out.
Bear safety

Glacier is grizzly and black bear country. The NPS calls bear spray the most effective deterrent and says hiking in groups significantly lowers your chances of a bad encounter. Bear bells aren't enough: calling out and clapping at regular intervals works better. It is prohibited to approach, view or do any activity within 100 yards (91 m) of bears or wolves. If you meet a bear, don't run; back away slowly. All food, containers, cookware and trash must be stored in a vehicle, a food locker or hung when not in use, day and night.
When to go

Glacier's hiking season is short. The NPS says Going-to-the-Sun Road has typically been fully open by early July, depending on snow; in 2026 it was expected to open on June 22. It typically stays fully open until the third Monday of October, weather permitting. The full road is about 50 miles and takes around 2 hours to drive. Between Avalanche Creek and Rising Sun, vehicles longer than 21 feet (including bumpers) or wider than 8 feet (including mirrors) are prohibited.
More mountain hikes
If you're heading north across the border, Banff National Park in the Canadian Rockies is another classic day-hiking destination with glaciers, lakes and big peaks.
See Banff National Park, with glacier-fed lakes and peaks of the Canadian Rockies.

Trail closures (including for bear activity), snow, road status and shuttle details change often. Always check current conditions and regulations with the National Park Service at nps.gov/glac before you go.

title: Trekking in the Annapurna region: when to go, permits and choosing your trek
lead: Seasons and the monsoon, the ACAP permit and TIMS card, the licensed-guide rule for foreign trekkers, and how the Circuit, Base Camp, Mardi Himal and Poon Hill compare, using official Nepali sources and CDC altitude guidance.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The Annapurna Conservation Area in central Nepal is one of the world's great trekking regions. The National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) launched the Annapurna Conservation Area Project (ACAP) in 1986. It covers 7,629 sq km and is the largest protected area in Nepal. It is also home to more than 100,000 people from many cultural and linguistic groups, so most treks here pass through villages as well as forests and high mountain country.

Pokhara, about 200 km west of Kathmandu, is the starting point for most Annapurna treks. Here's how to pick your season, sort out permits and choose a route, with every detail taken from official sources.
When to go: seasons and the monsoon

The Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) lists March to May and September to November as the best months for the Annapurna Conservation Area. Autumn, after the monsoon, usually brings the clearest skies and the best mountain views. Spring is rhododendron season, when the hillsides flower. NTB also notes that spring can bring seasonal rain and snowstorms.

The summer monsoon is the season most trekkers avoid. NTB warns that rain-soaked trails get slippery, so the monsoon is a poor time for trekking. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology gives 13 June and 2 October as the normal monsoon onset and withdrawal dates in eastern Nepal, about 112 days in all. Real years vary a lot. In 2025 the monsoon arrived on 29 May and didn't withdraw until 10 October. NTB notes that monsoon treks usually head to the drier rain-shadow areas of Manang and Mustang.
Winter is colder, with shorter days. NTB says heavier snowfall can sometimes close high passes. That matters on the Annapurna Circuit, which crosses one of the highest trekking passes in Nepal.
Photos from the trail
Permits: the ACAP entry permit and the TIMS card

Every Annapurna trek needs two documents. The first is the Annapurna Conservation Area entry permit, issued by NTNC. You can apply and pay online through NTNC's e-permit portal or get it at a permit counter. NTNC charges double the fee for permits issued at check-posts on the trail, so sort yours out before you set off. Each permit is valid for a single entry, and children under 10 don't need one. NTNC gets no regular government funding to run ACAP, and the entry fees are reinvested in the region and its communities.

The second is a TIMS (Trekkers' Information Management System) card. Under NTB's revised TIMS rules, in effect since 31 March 2023, the TIMS card for these routes is issued through a government-registered trekking agency. NTB lists the fee as NPR 2,000 for most foreign nationals and NPR 1,000 for citizens of South Asian (SAARC) countries. Upper Mustang is a restricted area and also needs a special trekking permit from the Department of Immigration.
The licensed-guide rule

Since the 2023 change, NTB says foreign trekkers on specified routes in protected areas must be accompanied by a licensed trekking guide and carry an agency-issued TIMS card. In the Annapurna region, NTB names the Annapurna Circuit, the Nar Phu and Mesokanto/Tilicho Pass variations, the Poon Hill and Annapurna Base Camp trek, Khopra, Mardi Himal and Sikleh Tara Hill. In practice, you book your trek through a registered agency, and the agency arranges your guide and TIMS card. Rules here have changed more than once, so confirm the current requirement with NTB before you book.
Choosing your trek

Annapurna Circuit. The classic loop around the Annapurna massif. NTB says it takes about three weeks at minimum to go all the way around. It usually runs counter-clockwise from Besi Sahar, off the Pokhara–Kathmandu highway. The route climbs through the Manang valley, crosses Thorong La at 5,416 m (about 17,770 feet) and drops to the pilgrimage town of Muktinath at 3,749 m (about 12,300 feet). It is the longest and highest of these options, so it needs the most time to acclimatize.
See the Annapurna Circuit on our map, with route details and photos from the trail over Thorong La.

Annapurna Base Camp (ABC). This trek heads into the Annapurna Sanctuary, an amphitheater of peaks that includes Annapurna I (8,091 m), Machhapuchhre (Fishtail) and Hiunchuli. NTB puts the base camp at 4,130 m (about 13,550 feet). Many trekkers combine it with Poon Hill.

Mardi Himal. NTB calls this route, opened in 2012, a quieter alternative. It climbs to Mardi Himal Base Camp at 4,500 m (about 14,760 feet), with close-up views of Machhapuchhre and the Annapurna range.

Ghorepani Poon Hill. NTB describes it as one of Nepal's most popular short treks and a good choice for beginners and families. The highlight is sunrise from Poon Hill at 3,210 m (about 10,530 feet), with Annapurna and Dhaulagiri lit up in gold. NTB notes that the Annapurna region offers short treks of around three days, so it suits a tighter schedule.
Pick your trek by the days you can give it, not the summit you want to photograph. Altitude doesn't care about your flight home.
Altitude safety

Three of these four treks go well above 4,000 m, and altitude illness is the biggest health risk. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that once you are above 3,000 m (9,800 feet), you raise your sleeping altitude by no more than 500 m (1,650 feet) a night. CDC also advises an extra night to acclimatize for every 1,000 m (3,300 feet) of sleeping altitude you gain. Build those rest days into your itinerary before you book, especially for the Circuit.

According to CDC, headache is the main symptom of acute mountain sickness, usually with one or more of loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue or nausea. Confusion, loss of coordination or unusual drowsiness can signal high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE). A cough and breathlessness that gets worse, even at rest, can signal high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). CDC's rules are clear: never go up to sleep at a higher altitude while you have symptoms, and descend if they get worse despite rest. CDC also covers preventive medication such as acetazolamide, so talk to a travel-medicine doctor before your trip.
The Everest region is the other classic Nepal trek — see our Everest Base Camp page for permits and the route from Lukla.

Trail conditions, permit rules, fees and weather in the Himalaya change often. Before you go, check current regulations and trail status with the Nepal Tourism Board (ntb.gov.np) and NTNC (epermit.ntnc.org.np), and check the latest health guidance with CDC.

title: How to plan the W Trek in Torres del Paine
lead: Park tickets, mandatory refugio and campsite bookings, which way to walk, how many days, when to go and how to reach Puerto Natales: a step-by-step plan for Patagonia's most famous multi-day hike, checked against CONAF and the park's official operators.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The W Trek is named for the shape it traces across the southern side of the Paine massif in Chilean Patagonia. It links the granite towers at Base Torres, the valley below Los Cuernos and Glacier Grey. The scenery gets the attention, but most of the work is in the planning. The trek is managed by CONAF, Chile's national forest service, and you can't just turn up with a tent. Here is the order we'd plan it in.
Step 1: Book your beds or tent sites first

This is the rule that catches most first-timers. CONAF says that to hike the W or the full Paine massif circuit (the O), you must book your overnight stays in advance. Without them you can't go into the mountain sector. The rule doesn't apply to day hikes such as Base Torres, to day trips along the road, or to the roadside campgrounds such as Camping Serrano and Camping Pehoé.

The refugios and campsites along the trail are run by two private operators, not by CONAF, and you book each one directly. Las Torres Patagonia (lastorres.com) runs the eastern and central sites, toward the towers and Los Cuernos. Vértice Patagonia (vertice.travel) runs Refugio & Camping Paine Grande, Refugio & Camping Grey, Refugio & Camping Dickson and Camping Los Perros. The last two are on the O circuit. Work out your nights first. Then book every stop before you buy flights, because each night has to line up with the next day's hike.

If you'd rather not piece it together yourself, Las Torres also sells a packaged W. It runs 5 days and 4 nights, or 4 days and 3 nights, with lodging, meals, park transport, the park entry ticket and the Lake Pehoé catamaran included. Its 2026–27 W departures run from October 2026 through April 2027.
Photos from the trail
Step 2: Buy your park entry ticket

Entry tickets are sold online through Pases Parques (pasesparques.cl), CONAF's official ticket portal. Your park ticket doesn't include a bed or a campsite. Those are booked separately (see Step 1). CONAF sells a day ticket and a multi-day ticket. For 2026 it lists the multi-day ticket for foreign adults at CLP 48,500. Children under 12, adults over 60 and people with disabilities get in free. Buy the ticket that matches the dates you booked.

CONAF lists park hours of 8:00 to 19:00, and hiking after dark is not allowed. For Base Torres, the 2026 schedule says you must start by 09:00 and be back down by 15:00. Times can change by season, so check the current schedule on the park's official site before you set your daily start times.
See Torres del Paine on the map, read our park overview and find more hikes in South America.
Step 3: Choose a direction and how many days

The W has two ends. The eastern end is the Torres sector, below the towers. The western end is Paine Grande, on Lake Pehoé, and from there a spur leads up to Glacier Grey. Paine Grande connects to the road by catamaran between Paine Grande and Pudeto. There is also a boat on Lake Grey. The Las Torres package walks east to west. It starts with a regular bus from Puerto Natales and ends with the Pehoé catamaran back toward town. Many hikers do the reverse. Choose a direction by what you can book: the order of your refugio or campsite nights decides it.

Las Torres sells the W in 4-day and 5-day versions. In our view, the extra day is worth it. It gives you room for a slower climb to the towers, and a spare half day if the weather turns. CONAF's daily trail report lists each W section as open or closed, along with any one-way-only stretches. Most one-way stretches are on the O, but check the report before you go.
Step 4: Pick your season, and respect the wind

The W is mainly a spring-to-autumn trip. Winter rules change things a lot. Under CONAF's 2026 winter rules, the W was open only with an accredited guide in May and August. It was closed completely in June and July. CONAF later kept the guide requirement through September 15 because of weather and trail conditions. From September 16, 2026, you no longer need a guide on the W or Base Torres. Microspikes and trekking poles may still be recommended or required while snow and ice remain. The O circuit stays closed through the winter, so check its reopening date with CONAF before planning a longer loop.

Patagonian weather changes fast, and CONAF can restrict or close trails when the forecast is bad. Its winter rules mention whiteout conditions on exposed passes. CONAF's advice is to check the forecast again and again while you're in the park. Pack a waterproof jacket and warm layers in every season. Keep your pack light enough to carry steadily in strong gusts. Allow some slack in your schedule, since a stormy day can mean waiting it out rather than pushing on.
Book the nights, then the ticket, then the flights, and leave room in the plan for Patagonia's weather.
Step 5: Getting to Puerto Natales and the park

Puerto Natales is the town where most W trips start and end. CONAF describes the route as a 250-kilometer paved road from Punta Arenas to Puerto Natales. From Puerto Natales you can reach the park on Route 9 North (about 150 km) or on the shorter Y-290 "Lago Porteño" road (about 80 km). The main entrances are Laguna Amarga, Sarmiento and Río Serrano.

CONAF's park page says regular buses leave Puerto Natales in the morning and the afternoon. Confirm the current timetable with the bus companies, and make sure your bus reaches the park in time for your first day's hike and your first night's booking. If your route uses the Pehoé catamaran, plan your return around its schedule.
Before you go

Stay on marked trails only. Lighting any fire or heat source outside permitted areas is banned and can bring heavy fines or prison time. Only approved camp stoves may be used, and only in designated areas. Pack out everything you bring in. If you want to see more of Patagonia after the W, Los Glaciares National Park, across the border in Argentina, makes a good second stop.
Continue to Los Glaciares, home of Fitz Roy and the Perito Moreno Glacier.

Rules, fees, trail status and seasonal closures in Torres del Paine change often, sometimes within a season. Always check current conditions and regulations with CONAF at parquetorresdelpaine.cl and conaf.cl, and confirm your bookings directly with the operators before you travel.

title: Walking the Milford Track: a complete guide
lead: Four days, three huts and one direction through the heart of Fiordland: how bookings, transport, huts and weather work on New Zealand's most famous Great Walk, straight from the Department of Conservation.
author: Great Hikes

blocks.text: The Milford Track runs from the head of Lake Te Anau to Sandfly Point on Milford Sound/Piopiotahi, through Fiordland National Park on New Zealand's South Island. The Department of Conservation (DOC) lists it as a 54 km (about 33.5 mile) walk over four days and three nights. It follows glacier-carved valleys and ancient beech forest, climbs over an alpine pass and passes some of the country's most famous waterfalls.

It is also one of the most tightly managed walks in the world. You can't drive to either end, you can't camp, and you can only walk it one way. Here's how it all fits together, with the details as DOC publishes them.
Season and bookings

The Great Walks season for 2026/27 runs from 1 November 2026 to 30 April 2027, with the last departure on 28 April 2027. During the season you must book all three huts in advance through the DOC booking system. Bookings for 2026/27 opened on 13 May 2026, and DOC says they are open now. Milford dates are in high demand, so check availability early and have backup dates ready.

DOC's own booking tips are simple: create your DOC booking account well before you need it, test your login before an opening day, read the rules for your track, and have a plan B if your first choice is full.

Hut fees are charged per person, per night. For the 2026/27 Great Walks season DOC lists NZ$106 for New Zealand adults and NZ$152 for international adults. Children pay NZ$53 (New Zealand, ages 5–17) or NZ$76 (international, ages 0–17), and New Zealand infants (0–4) stay free. Outside the season, the fee drops to NZ$30 per adult and NZ$15 per child. Fees change, so confirm them when you book.
Photos from the trail
One direction, three huts, no camping

The Milford Track can only be walked one way, from Glade Wharf to Sandfly Point. Camping is not permitted. Walkers stay in three DOC huts in order: Clinton Hut, then Mintaro Hut, then Dumpling Hut. For safety, DOC requires you to stay in each hut on the night shown on your booking confirmation.

Each hut has 40 bunks with mattresses in shared rooms. In the Great Walks season they have heating, toilets, basic cooking facilities with fuel, solar lighting and cold running water, and a DOC ranger lives on site. There are no showers and no cooking utensils, so bring your own pots, plates and cutlery. Outside the season, gas is not provided and the running water is turned off, so you need your own stove.
Explore Fiordland National Park on the map and see photos of Milford Sound from our community.
Getting there from Te Anau

There is no vehicle or private access to either end of the track, so you must book your transport in advance. From Te Anau, take a bus or private transport to Te Anau Downs (about 30 minutes). From there, a boat takes you to Glade Wharf at the head of Lake Te Anau (1 hour 15 minutes). At the end, a 20-minute boat ride runs from Sandfly Point to Milford Sound/Piopiotahi, where bus services connect back to Te Anau and on to Queenstown. DOC also points to guided walks on the track if you'd rather not go independently.
The track, day by day

Day 1: Glade Wharf to Clinton Hut, 5 km (about 3 miles), 1 to 1.5 hours. After the boat cruise, it's an easy walk through beech forest beside the Clinton River. DOC notes a short Wetland Walkway near the hut, about 15 minutes return.

Day 2: Clinton Hut to Mintaro Hut, 17.5 km (about 11 miles), about 6 hours. A gradual climb follows the Clinton River to its source at Lake Mintaro, at the foot of Omanui/McKinnon Pass. On the way you pass Hirere Falls and get views of the Pompolona icefield.

Day 3: Mintaro Hut to Dumpling Hut, 13 km (about 8 miles), 6 to 7 hours. This is the big day. You climb to Omanui/McKinnon Pass, the highest point of the track at 1,154 m (about 3,786 feet), then descend around 1,000 m through alpine gardens and past waterfalls along the Roaring Burn. DOC calls the side trip to Sutherland Falls a definite highlight. It takes about 1 hour 30 minutes return, and the falls drop 580 m (about 1,900 feet) in three leaps from Lake Quill.

Day 4: Dumpling Hut to Sandfly Point, 18 km (about 11 miles), 5.5 to 6 hours. You follow the Arthur River past the historic Boatshed, Mackay Falls and Bell Rock. The last 3 km is a smooth, wide track built by a prison labour gang between 1890 and 1892, ending at the boat to Milford Sound.
Book the huts and both boats before anything else, then pack for rain, whatever month it is.
Weather and safety

Fiordland is one of the wettest places in New Zealand. DOC notes rainfall of up to 9,000 mm (about 354 inches) a year, and warns that cold temperatures, snow, strong winds and heavy rain can happen at any time of year. Both the Clinton and Arthur valleys become impassable in heavy rain. Pack a good waterproof jacket and warm layers even in midsummer, and keep your gear dry in a pack liner. There is no cellphone coverage on the track.

Avalanche risk can extend into December, and DOC counts more than 57 avalanche paths along the route. Outside the Great Walks season (May to late October), the track is not managed. DOC says it should only be attempted by fit, experienced and well-equipped people, with alpine gear such as an ice axe and crampons, plus an avalanche beacon, snow shovel and probe. DOC also does not recommend the track for children under 10, because of the exposed mountain terrain and frequent bad weather.
More Great Walks

If Milford dates are full, or you'd like a gentler coastal walk, the Abel Tasman Coast Track at the top of the South Island is another DOC Great Walk. Note that its huts and campsites must be booked in advance all year round.
See Abel Tasman National Park, with golden beaches and coastal forest at the top of the South Island.
Track conditions, closures, fees and transport change often. Always check current track alerts, weather and regulations with the Department of Conservation at doc.govt.nz/milfordtrack before you go.
